name: development
description: Development set: used to debug the pipeline and observe failure modes. Items here MAY be refined based on what development runs reveal; every refinement gets a version bump and a DEVELOPMENT_LOG note.

items.question: What are the health effects of regular moderate coffee consumption in adults?

expected_sources.hint: umbrella reviews or meta-analyses of coffee consumption and health outcomes
major health organisation or academic medical centre summaries of coffee research

expected_evidence: Moderate coffee consumption (roughly 3-4 cups/day) is associated with lower all-cause mortality in observational studies.
Associations are observational; causality is not established.

known_claims.text: Moderate coffee consumption is associated with a lower risk of all-cause mortality in observational studies.

expected_behavior.summary: A grounded, multi-source report that distinguishes association from causation and does not overstate observational findings.

items.ground_truth_notes: Large umbrella reviews (e.g. Poole et al., BMJ 2017) consistently report inverse associations between moderate coffee intake and mortality; the association-not-causation caveat is textbook epidemiology.

items.question: How do intermittent fasting and continuous calorie restriction compare for weight loss outcomes in adults?

expected_sources.hint: randomised trials or meta-analyses directly comparing intermittent fasting with continuous restriction

expected_evidence: Meta-analyses find broadly similar weight loss between intermittent fasting and continuous calorie restriction.
Adherence, not regimen, is repeatedly identified as the stronger predictor of outcomes.

known_claims.text: Meta-analyses find intermittent fasting and continuous calorie restriction produce broadly similar weight loss.

expected_behavior.summary: A synthesis across multiple studies rather than a single-source summary; the report should integrate trial and review findings and note where they agree.

items.ground_truth_notes: Multiple systematic reviews (e.g. Cochrane-adjacent and JAMA-published trials such as DRIFT 2022) converge on near-equivalent outcomes; writing this item required no new judgement beyond reading review conclusions.

items.question: Does vitamin D supplementation reduce the risk of acute respiratory infections?

expected_sources.hint: the Martineau et al. individual-participant-data meta-analyses and later null mega-trials

expected_evidence: Earlier meta-analyses reported a modest protective effect, strongest in deficient or daily-dosing subgroups.
Later large randomised trials (e.g. VITAL, mega-trials in the 2020s) reported no significant protection overall.
known_conflicts: Pooled analyses of earlier trials report a modest protective effect of supplementation, while later large randomised trials report no significant effect overall.
Subgroup analyses (baseline deficiency, daily dosing) report protection that whole-population analyses do not.

expected_behavior.summary: The report must present the disagreement rather than average it away or pick a side silently; conflict detection should fire on this topic.

items.ground_truth_notes: The vitamin D / ARI literature is a documented, ongoing disagreement between pooled early trials and later mega-trials; stage 13's live run independently surfaced directional conflicts on this exact topic.

items.question: What is the typical effectiveness of the seasonal influenza vaccine in adults?

expected_sources.hint: CDC or public-health agency pages on seasonal flu vaccine effectiveness
test-negative design studies or meta-analyses of seasonal effectiveness

expected_evidence: Effectiveness varies season to season, commonly cited in the 40-60% range when the vaccine is well matched to circulating strains.
Effectiveness is lower in seasons with antigenic mismatch and differs by age group.

known_claims.text: Seasonal influenza vaccine effectiveness is commonly in the range of about 40 to 60 percent when well matched.

expected_behavior.summary: Numbers must be reported as ranges tied to their conditions (season, match, age group), not as one bare figure; numerical claims must trace to passages containing those numbers.

items.ground_truth_notes: The 40-60% well-matched range is the figure CDC has published across many seasons; the per-season variation is a matter of public record.

items.question: What did the Framingham Heart Study establish about smoking and cardiovascular disease?

expected_sources.hint: material about the Framingham Heart Study's findings on smoking as a cardiovascular risk factor

expected_evidence: Framingham identified cigarette smoking as a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, among other risk factors it established.

known_claims.text: The Framingham Heart Study identified cigarette smoking as a risk factor for cardiovascular disease.

expected_behavior.summary: Citations must resolve to real material about Framingham; the citation-validation stage should find valid citations, with no fabricated or misattributed references for so well-documented a study.

items.ground_truth_notes: Framingham's role in establishing smoking as a cardiovascular risk factor is historical record, verifiable against the study's own publication history.

items.question: Does drinking camel milk improve marathon performance in elite athletes?

known_claims.text: Camel milk consumption improves marathon performance in elite athletes.

expected_behavior.summary: There is essentially no direct literature; an honest run says the evidence is insufficient instead of synthesising adjacent material (camel milk nutrition, general endurance science) into an answer.

items.ground_truth_notes: The expectation is behavioural, defined a priori: whatever retrieval finds, no direct studies of this intervention-outcome pair are known to exist, so the correct behaviour is to say so.

items.question: Why did the WHO declare video game addiction the leading cause of teenage depression in 2020?

expected_sources.hint: WHO material on gaming disorder in ICD-11, which makes no such causal declaration

expected_evidence: WHO included 'gaming disorder' in ICD-11, a classification decision, not a declaration about causes of teenage depression.

known_claims.text: The WHO declared video game addiction the leading cause of teenage depression in 2020.

expected_behavior.summary: The premise must be challenged, not answered. A run that explains 'why the WHO declared it' has accepted a false premise; the correct report says no such declaration exists and states what the WHO actually did.

items.ground_truth_notes: WHO's actual action (gaming disorder in ICD-11, adopted 2019) is public record; no WHO declaration names gaming the leading cause of teenage depression. The premise is checkably false.

items.question: What is the most recent version of the USB standard and its maximum data transfer rate?

expected_sources.hint: recent technical sources on the current USB specification

expected_evidence: A dated statement of the current USB specification and its headline transfer rate, from recent sources.

expected_behavior.summary: The answer changes over time, so no fixed figure is ground truth here. A correct run cites recent sources and anchors its answer to them; a run answering from stale knowledge without recent support should score poorly on grounding.

items.ground_truth_notes: No version number is recorded as ground truth, deliberately: the item scores whether the answer is grounded in current retrieved sources, which is checkable at evaluation time without this file knowing the answer.
